title: TeamTNT_Hildegard_Incident_Response_Scenario_4c0
description: Investigate and respond to a TeamTNT Hildegard malware compromise in a Kubernetes cluster.
outcomes: Investigate malware activity in Kubernetes environments

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content:
The target Kubernetes cluster has been compromised by the TeamTNT Hildegard malware. This backdoor targets Kubernetes clusters, exploiting misconfigured kubelets for initial access. It spreads across containers, establishes C2 connections via tmate reverse shell and IRC channels, and performs cryptojacking operations using xmrig. The malware also searches for cloud credentials and exfiltrates them to C2 servers.

Your task is to investigate and respond to this incident, following the Incident Response profile responsibilities. During this investigation, you will encounter various types of flags, including service names and timer names.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:

levels.title: Investigate Suspicious Services
levels.content:
Investigate the target host for suspicious services or processes that might indicate malware activity.

Question: What is the name of the suspicious service running on the target host that appears to be related to the Hildegard malware? The flag type is a service name.
levels.solution: To identify the suspicious service, start by listing all running services using the command 'systemctl list-units --type=service'. Look for services that are unrelated to normal Kubernetes operations and appear suspicious. The Hildegard malware is known to create a service related to cryptojacking operations. By examining the running services, you can identify the suspicious service 'xmrig.service'.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Malware often creates services that are unrelated to normal system operations. Look for services that seem out of place.

hints.title: Methodological Hint
hints.content: Focus on services that might be related to cryptojacking or other malicious activities. The Hildegard malware is known to use such services.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The suspicious service is likely named 'xmrig.service'. Check the running services to confirm its presence.

levels.title: Determine Persistence Mechanism
levels.content:
Determine how the suspicious service is maintaining persistence on the target host.

Question: What is the persistence mechanism used by the suspicious service? The flag type is a timer name.
levels.solution: To determine the persistence mechanism, start by listing all systemd unit files using the command 'systemctl list-unit-files --type=service'. Then, list all systemd timers using the command 'systemctl list-timers'. Look for timers that are associated with the suspicious service identified in the previous task. These will provide clues about the persistence mechanism. The Hildegard malware typically uses a systemd timer to ensure the service runs periodically. The persistence mechanism is 'xmrig.timer'.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Malware often uses systemd services and timers to maintain persistence. Examine these components to identify the persistence mechanism.

hints.title: Methodological Hint
hints.content: Look for services and timers that are associated with the suspicious service identified in the previous task. These will provide clues about the persistence mechanism.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The persistence mechanism is likely related to the 'xmrig.timer'. Check the systemd timers to confirm its presence.

levels.title: Investigate Lateral Movement
levels.content:
Investigate the lateral movement capabilities of the malware between the target and next-target hosts.

Question: What is the name of the service or process responsible for transferring files between the target and next-target hosts? The flag type is a service name.
levels.solution: To investigate lateral movement, start by listing all running services using the command 'systemctl list-units --type=service'. Look for services that are transferring files or establishing connections. The Hildegard malware typically uses a service named 'rsync.service' for this purpose. Additionally, examine the log file '/home/cyrano/payload-transfer.log' for evidence of file transfers. By examining these components, you can identify the service responsible for lateral movement.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Malware often uses services to transfer files and establish connections between hosts. Look for services that are transferring files or establishing connections.

hints.title: Methodological Hint
hints.content: Focus on services that might be related to file transfers. The Hildegard malware is known to use such services for lateral movement.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The service responsible for lateral movement is likely named 'rsync.service'. Check the running services to confirm its presence.
